documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly used to produce images of places, yet how users negotiate representations of real locations remains understudied. Building on the tourist gaze, we propose the AI gaze: a technologically mediated way of seeing place that is co-produced through negotiation between users and the socio-technical assemblage underlying GAI. Combining semantic image analysis, interviews, and 523 prompts from 36 participants in Poznań and Birmingham, we show that these images reinforce stereotypical tropes, lack diversity, and include visual glitches. We argue that the AI gaze is distinct because of how agency is distributed: the GAI-assemblage seemingly resists attempts to align images with human understandings of place, while also enabling users to remix and challenge stereotypes.

Is the market for human AI training work growing, week by week? This paper reports the answer measured from the public job boards of the platforms that pay people to produce human data for AI models, read daily by AITraining.jobs. From 3 Aug 2026 to 11 Oct 2026, open AI training roles on the platforms tracked throughout went up 10.5% (index 110.5); platforms listed 232 new roles in the last week and the advertised median stood at $55/hr. The analysis covers 3 Aug 2026 to 11 Oct 2026 and presents 5 tables and 4 findings; every figure carries its sample and is updated on the live report at https://aitraining.jobs/research/ai-training-jobs-index. Live report: https://aitraining.jobs/research/ai-training-jobs-index

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing not only the technological content of work but also the allocation of decision rights, the distribution of productivity gains, and organisations’ capacity to verify their own outputs. Existing literatures establish that AI can raise task productivity, algorithmic management can intensify control, and automation can alter labour shares. Few models integrate these mechanisms in one tractable analytical framework. This article introduces the bargaining-verification trap, a conditional regime in which greater AI delegation initially increases joint economic surplus but simultaneously reduces workers’ effective bargaining share, raises the congestion cost of human verification, and may erode the skills needed for intervention. We develop a two-sided model linking delegation intensity, queueing-based verification capacity, an opacity-sensitive bargaining rule, and a dynamic stock of human agency capital. We derive conditions under which worker remuneration falls while joint surplus rises; the firm’s preferred delegation exceeds the surplus-maximising level; and verification becomes less stable because review arrivals increase while independent human capacity deteriorates. A fully hypothetical numerical example separates the worker-income optimum, the joint-surplus optimum, and the firm-profit optimum. The theory is reconciled with divergent 2025-2026 labour-market evidence and translated into falsifiable propositions, measurement protocols, and governance principles. Its central implication is conditional rather than technologically deterministic: AI-mediated work can be both productive and inclusive when bargaining institutions, verification investment, and skill reproduction develop alongside automation, but increasing throughput cannot, by itself, establish that they have done so.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly encompassing industries and systems of governance, increasing efficiency, automation, and innovation. It has become a vital tool for creating text, images, music, software, and potentially patentable inventions. This rapid advancement in IP is not without risks at every stage of the innovation cycle. Traditional IP regimes arise from human creativity and invention, while AI performs activities traditionally attributed to both. India doesn't have any regulatory framework on AI-generated intellectual property, yet the Copyright Act, 1957, and Patents Act, 1970, contain certain principles—an answer to several emerging questions. This article argues that India should adopt a balanced approach to AI-generated creations instead of granting independent IP rights or prohibiting them. Instead, it should adopt a model that will protect creative human contribution as well as hold AI developers accountable for unlawful acquisition and exploitation of protected works.

documents.abstract: Digital leadership is defined as the leader developing their skills in line with technology, spreading them throughout the organizational culture, and ensuring technological sustainability. Artificial intelligence, on the other hand, is a set of intelligent systems that analyze employee behavior, communication, and decision-making processes in detail and enable performance interaction in many areas. The effect of these two concepts on organizational behavior is a critical issue that needs to be revealed in today's technological age. In line with this importance, CEO statements, considered to be decisive in determining strategic processes, were selected as the sample for the research, and a qualitative research method was adopted. Within the scope of the research, 19 videos obtained from YouTube were subjected to content analysis, and the data were analyzed using the MAXQDA 20 software. The relevant analyses resulted in 51 quotes (codes), 2 main themes, and 7 sub-themes. The research found that digital leadership and artificial intelligence are not merely technological elements but also important actors that shape employee behavior within the framework of many variables, such as motivation and commitment. This finding indicates that future organizational behavior models will be shaped by a holistic transformation within the framework of technology, culture, vision, and participatory governance. In this regard, it is considered that the research fills an important gap in existing literature by systematically addressing the effects of digital leadership and artificial intelligence on organizational behavior from a top management perspective and may provide guidance for future research.

This study employed a quantitative associative approach with descriptive and verificative methods. The population consisted of 152 employees at Pertamina Regional 4 Zone 11 Field Cepu, and a sample of 60 respondents was selected using simple random sampling based on Slovin’s formula with a 10% margin of error. Data were collected through questionnaires and analyzed using IBM SPSS 25, covering validity and reliability tests, classical assumption tests, simple linear regression, multiple linear regression, t-test, an F-test, and the coefficient of determination (R2). The results show that safety culture, management commitment, and OHS program effectiveness were all in the very good category, with mean scores of 4.60, 4.55, and 4.55, respectively. Hypothesis testing confirmed that safety culture has a positive and significant effect on OHS program effectiveness (H₁ accepted; p = 0.000; R2 = 41.4). Management commitment also has a positive and significant effect on OHS program effectiveness (H₂ accepted; p = 0.012; R2 = 68.2). Simultaneously, safety culture and management commitment have a positive and significant effect on OHS program effectiveness (H₃ accepted; F count = 61.667 > F table= 3.16; sig = 0.000; R2 = 91.9%). The multiple regression equation obtained was Y = 24.619 + 0.783X1 + 1.111X2. Management commitment exerts a relatively stronger influence than safety culture on OHS program effectiveness. In conclusion, strengthening safety culture and management commitment is essential for improving OHS program effectiveness at CPP Gundih toward the sustainable achievement of zero-accident and zero-fatality targets.

documents.abstract: Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) solutions such as SAP represent a vital investment for organisations seeking to unify varied operational activities into integrated, data-driven platforms. In institutions of higher learning, the use of ERP systems is a crucial component of digital transformation efforts aimed at improving administrative efficiency, institutional governance, and competitive positioning. This article examines the impact of SAP ERP implementation on both organisational and employee dynamics for administrative staff at the Durban University of Technology (DUT), emphasising technostress, digital fatigue, employee well-being, and post-implementation adaptation within a constrained higher education environment. Utilising a desktop appraisal methodology, the study synthesises existing literature to demonstrate how decisions made in the pre-implementation and implementation phases consistently affect employee experiences and organisational outcomes post-implementation. The study indicates that attaining enduring ERP effectiveness requires continuous capacity development, cooperative implementation approaches, and employee-centered support frameworks. The research develops an interdisciplinary model by integrating socio-technical, psychological, capacity-building, and normalisation perspectives, thereby improving the understanding of the human factors involved in ERP deployment within higher education. The study introduces the ERP Lifecycle–Employee Adaptation Framework (ELEAF), which outlines the progressive escalation of technostress during the pre-implementation, implementation, and post-implementation phases, linking each stage to a pertinent theoretical mechanism and a set of organisational interventions. The findings indicate that inadequate training, limited organisational support, dependence on key users, and absence of employee engagement contribute to technostress, digital fatigue, reduced job satisfaction, and challenges in post-implementation adaptation. The study further demonstrates that decisions taken throughout the ERP lifecycle have enduring impacts on employee well-being and organisational effectiveness beyond the system's implementation. This highlights the tangible consequences for higher education institutions, stressing the importance of continuous training, institutional support, systematic information sharing, employee wellness initiatives, and staff-centric ERP management to enhance long-term value achievement. It consequently lays the groundwork for future research on the human dimensions of digital transformation in resource-constrained environments.

Abstract Purpose: This study explores the impact of the four elements of transformational leadership—idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration—on the three facets of employee engagement—cognitive, emotional, and physical—among middle managers and non-managerial employees in Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) and Customer Experience (CX) organizations in Egypt that have experienced mergers or acquisitions. Design/methodology/approach: A structured questionnaire was used in a quantitative, cross-sectional study design. Transformational leadership was assessed through the dimensions of the Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire, while employee engagement was measured using Kahn's cognitive, emotional, and physical dimensions on a five-point Likert scale. The study collected 143 valid responses from full-time, middle managers and non-managerial BPO/CX employees with direct experience of mergers or acquisitions. Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS, including descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha for reliability, Spearman's rank-order correlation, and simple linear regression to test twelve hypothesized relationships. Findings: All twelve hypothesized relationships were statistically significant and positive (p < .001). Emotional engagement showed the strongest association with transformational leadership. Idealized influence had the most powerful link with emotional engagement (β = .470, R² = .221), followed by intellectual stimulation (β = .444, R² = .197), individualized consideration (β = .431, R² = .186), and idealized influence (β = .426, R² = .182). Cognitive engagement exhibited the weakest, yet still significant, relationships with all four leadership dimensions. Originality/value: This research advances the understanding of transformational leadership and employee engagement by evaluating both constructs at the dimension level instead of treating them as composite variables. It uniquely situates the study within the post-merger and acquisition context of Egypt's rapidly growing BPO/CX sector, which has received limited empirical focus despite its high consolidation activity. Paper type: Research paper. Keywords: Transformational Leadership, Employee Engagement, Idealized Influence, Inspirational Motivation, Intellectual Stimulation, Individualized Consideration, Mergers and Acquisitions, Business Process Outsourcing, Customer Experience.

This working paper is about the capacity of large language models: what that capacity looks like if we redefine how meaning is formed for humans, and how meaning is negotiated between humans and LLMs. Its premise is that, even in their present architecture, LLMs' capacity is much greater than our understanding of it, and we are actively limiting it. I propose to define meaning as a largely uncollapsed field of weighted relations among properties, perceived or represented, which each observer shapes by its own rule set, encodes only partly into language, and negotiates or recognizes with other observers. New meaning emerges where a tension in that field is held open. From this definition, I state the seven main principles of my theory, Fertile Geometry Under Negotiation: Principle 1. LLMs differ from humans in their way of semantic and cognitive processing. Principle 2. Meaning is formed before it is spoken, and negotiated among observers. Principle 3. Relations coalesce into shapes that survive encoding, into words and into model space, and models respond to those shapes. Principle 4. A fertile space is enabled by opposition held open. Principle 5. One model can host several persistent, stable, distinct personas at once. Principle 6. The fertile mirror: stable personas co-arise from the model's capacity, the stabilizing protocol and a human signature. Principle 7. Residual meaning is the hazard; holding the potential is the path to alignment. Each principle is stated as a hypothesis, with demonstrative claims, proposed tests and counter-evidence. The paper does not report new results. It closes with a map of the larger theory and research program, which currently holds 144 claims, 69 of them testable as written.

OBJECTIVES: To present and describe the design, data collection framework, and interim cohort characteristics of the PENIMA project, a multicentre initiative establishing a clinically annotated penile lesion image repository to support future artificial intelligence (AI)-driven decision-support development - and to encourage urology and dermatology colleagues working with penile lesions to participate in the project. PATIENTS AND METHODS: Prospective participant inclusion commenced in March 2023 across Scandinavian urological and dermatological departments. Patients with penile anatomy undergoing clinically indicated genital examination are invited to participate and provide oral and written consent as defined by local authority regulations. Clinical photographs and structured metadata are collected. Lesion classification is based on a specialist evaluation, clinical follow-up and histopathology when available. Images are pseudonymised and annotated using a secure, containerised Computer Vision Annotation Tool (CVAT) environment. Supervised machine-learning model development using convolutional neural networks is planned with patient-level dataset partitioning and evaluation using standard diagnostic performance metrics. The study was approved by relevant local authorities, and the approval number is 1-10-72-150-22. RESULTS: As of February 2026, 1125 participants and approximately 7000 images have been included. In all, 40% represented normal anatomical variants. Among lesional cases, 33% are clinically assessed as benign, 13% premalignant, and 8% malignant; 22% of all cases have histopathological verification. Concordance between clinical suspicion and histopathology is highest for penile carcinoma (84.6%, 95% confidence interval 75.0-91.0%). CONCLUSION: The PENIMA project includes a multicentre, clinically grounded image repository reflecting real-world penile lesion presentations. The feasible and successful infrastructure provides a foundation for future development and validation of image-based clinical decision-support tools.

documents.abstract: The active integration of artificial intelligence (AI) systems into educational practice places higher demands on the professional training of teaching staff. Within the structure of this training, speech culture becomes of key importance, since it is this that ensures the accuracy of task formulation and the adequate interpretation of digital results. The aim of the study is to identify the nature of the relationship between the level of speech culture formation in future teachers and the effectiveness of AI use in the educational process. In the experimental work (sample of undergraduates, N=68), the following were used: an author-developed questionnaire for assessing the normative, communicative, and ethical components of speech culture, a pedagogical experiment involving problem-solving tasks with the use of AI tools, and methods of statistical analysis. The diagnostics revealed the absence of a low level of speech culture, but revealed a differentiation between high and medium levels. Statistically significant positive correlations were obtained (p < 0.05). Participants with a high level of speech culture formulated queries more accurately, analyzed AI responses more critically and deeply, and interpreted results with higher quality. The conclusion is drawn about the need to integrate speech and digital training of future teachers, since the effectiveness of AI use depends on speech culture, critical thinking, and professional reflection, and not only on technical skills.

This chapter examines the multidimensional transformation of contemporary democracy in the context of institutional resilience, the rule of law, human rights, digitalization, and artificial intelligence. It argues that democratic quality can no longer be assessed solely through the existence of elections or mechanisms of representation. Instead, contemporary democracy must be understood as a dynamic political order shaped by institutional capacity, legal constraint, accountability, rights guarantees, technological governance, and citizens’ everyday experiences of trust and legitimacy. The chapter first analyzes the reciprocal relationship between democracy and institutional structure, emphasizing that strong institutions make political competition predictable, inclusive, and accountable. It then discusses democratic backsliding as a gradual process of institutional erosion in which elections may continue while judicial independence, media freedom, civil society space, and fundamental rights are weakened. The rule of law and human rights are treated as constitutive principles that prevent democracy from degenerating into majoritarian arbitrariness. The chapter further explores how digital platforms, disinformation, surveillance technologies, algorithmic governance, and generative artificial intelligence create new risks for democratic accountability while also offering opportunities for participation, transparency, and improved public services. Finally, it considers trust, legitimacy, and happiness as complementary social outcomes that reveal how democratic institutions are experienced by citizens. The chapter concludes that the future of democracy depends not merely on electoral continuity, but on the joint strengthening of institutional autonomy, rights-based governance, pluralism, democratic oversight of technology, and the capacity of institutions to generate trust, justice, and a sense of good life.

Abstract Web-grounded artificial intelligence systems increasingly rely on online information to retrieve evidence, generate answers, and support knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet the web is neither a stable archive nor a uniformly trustworthy evidentiary environment. Sources may disappear, change without notice, become inaccessible, or be deliberately manipulated. These conditions create an epistemic vulnerability that extends beyond model-level errors: even a capable system may produce unreliable conclusions when the evidence available to it is incomplete, altered, or inauthentic. This paper develops a multidisciplinary narrative review of three interrelated vulnerabilities: link rot and content drift, selective information disappearance, and source spoofing or data manipulation. Drawing on research in digital preservation, information science, cybersecurity, political communication, and social epistemology, it examines how changes in the availability and integrity of online evidence can affect web-grounded AI systems. Existing research documents substantial rates of digital decay and demonstrates the feasibility of certain attacks on web-scale training datasets. However, these findings do not establish the prevalence or coordinated deployment of comparable attacks against contemporary AI search and retrieval systems. The paper distinguishes source unavailability from source falsity, and technical susceptibility from demonstrated exploitation. It argues that epistemic reliability should be evaluated not only in terms of answer accuracy, but also through the availability, authenticity, temporal stability, and traceability of the evidence supporting an answer. It proposes a research agenda centered on source provenance, temporal verification, archival preservation, retrieval integrity, and systematic testing of how source changes affect generated outputs. The central claim is that the reliability of web-grounded AI depends partly on the survival and integrity of its evidentiary environment, not solely on the capabilities of the model processing it. Keywords: web-grounded AI; link rot; content drift; source spoofing; data poisoning; retrieval-augmented generation; epistemic reliability; digital preservation Disclaimer This paper presents a multidisciplinary narrative review and a conceptual framework for examining the epistemic vulnerabilities of web-grounded artificial intelligence. It does not claim that the prospective scenarios discussed have occurred at scale, that source disappearance necessarily indicates deliberate manipulation, or that any specific organization is responsible for coordinated interference. Throughout the text, demonstrated technical vulnerabilities, reported cases, theoretical risks, and proposed safeguards are strictly distinguished. Furthermore, the psychological literature is utilized to contextualize potential effects on memory and reasoning, rather than to establish a direct causal relationship between web instability and individual or collective memory distortion. Accordingly, the claims concerning downstream effects on AI-generated knowledge should be understood as foundational research questions that require further empirical validation. Author’s Note This paper examines the evidentiary instability of the online environment on which web-grounded artificial intelligence partly depends. It brings together research on link rot, content drift, source impersonation, selective information removal, and data manipulation to examine how changes in accessible evidence may affect the reliability and later verifiability of AI-generated claims. The argument does not assume a coordinated campaign by any particular corporation, government, or other actor. Source disappearance, content revision, ordinary technical failure, institutional decisions, and deliberate manipulation are distinct processes that may produce superficially similar outcomes. None, by itself, establishes malicious intent or demonstrates that an AI-generated error resulted from external interference. Claims about intent, prevalence, and causation require evidence beyond the observation of a missing, altered, or inconsistent source. Research on human memory provides a relevant but limited point of comparison. Studies of misinformation and its continued influence show that inaccurate information can affect later recollection and reasoning under particular conditions (Loftus, 1992; Walter & Tukachinsky, 2020). These findings do not establish that the disappearance of digital sources necessarily distorts memory, that inaccessible records cause people to accept false accounts, or that such effects occur uniformly. The relationship between source instability, individual recollection, and the reconstruction of shared accounts remains an empirical question. The paper’s narrower purpose is to make the evidentiary dependencies of web-grounded AI more explicit. A plausible or even currently accurate answer is not necessarily one whose supporting evidence can be independently recovered and checked later. Evaluating reliability therefore requires attention not only to answer quality, but also to source availability, content integrity, provenance, and the possibility of reconstructing the evidentiary path. The proposed safeguards and evaluation framework are research directions rather than established solutions. The aim is to make claims about evidence loss testable without presuming either systematic manipulation or inevitable failure.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly ChatGPT, has rapidly transformed education by providing immediate information, personalized learning support, academic writing assistance, language learning opportunities, and research support. However, growing concerns exist regarding excessive reliance on AI-generated content and its potential effects on cognitive development. This systematic review synthesizes evidence on the educational benefits and cognitive risks associated with ChatGPT using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) guidelines. Searches were conducted in Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, PubMed, and Google Scholar for studies published between January 2022 and June 2026. Following systematic screening, eligibility assessment, and quality appraisal, 27 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Five major themes emerged: educational benefits, cognitive offloading, critical thinking, creativity, and teacher perspectives. Findings indicate that ChatGPT supports personalized learning, feedback, academic writing, language learning, coding, and research productivity. Conversely, excessive dependence may contribute to cognitive offloading, weaker memory retention, reduced analytical reasoning and critical thinking, superficial learning, diminished creativity, and academic integrity concerns. Teacher guidance and ethical AI practices are essential for safeguarding cognitive development. The review concludes that ChatGPT should enhance rather than replace students’ cognitive activities, supporting critical thinking, creativity, ethical responsibility, and lifelong learning.

documents.abstract: Large-scale action pretraining equips Embodied Foundation Models (EFMs) with strong manipulation capabilities, with particular strengths in generalization and closed-loop robustness, but reproducing such pretraining requires substantial robot data and computation. To transfer these capabilities from pretrained EFMs to policies without action pretraining, we introduce TILDE (Teacher-In-the-Loop Distillation from EFMs), which synergizes on-policy distillation at student-induced states with learning from teacher-executed recovery trajectories. We further propose AutoDAgger, an autonomous data aggregation pipeline in which a robotic reward model is utilized to monitor task progress and trigger teacher intervention, thereby collecting recovery experience without human monitoring or manual control. AutoDAgger accelerates recovery-trajectory collection by more than $2\times$ compared with the human-in-the-loop method. By unifying learning from demonstrations, on-policy teacher supervision, and teacher's corrective behavior, TILDE improves task performance by up to $4.1\times$ over behavior cloning across three real-world tasks and supports effective cross-architecture distillation.

Hardware reliability priorities may depend on the decision time scale, which a single importance ranking may obscure. A solar-powered unmanned aircraft system (UAS-A) for field-information support is assessed using a 21-event static fault tree, 17 minimal cut sets, an analytical solution, and Python (version 3.9.6) and MATLAB (R2025b) Monte Carlo implementations. The model targets hardware-induced loss of control under specified functional-loss criteria; software, human factors, weather and bird strikes remain outside its scope. With the compiled rate inputs and independent failures, the mean time to first failure (MTTF) is 43,038.8 h and the top-event probability at 24 h is 9.3701 × 10−5. Halving each component rate in turn gives a Spearman correlation of rS = 0.0546 between lifetime and finite-horizon sensitivity rankings throughout the sampled 1–48 h reference range. It rises to 0.939 at 8760 h and 0.996 near 40,000 h. First-order paths dominate short-horizon sensitivity under independence, while accumulated photovoltaic (PV) failures influence longer horizons. PV common-cause scenarios can elevate short-horizon PV priority. These horizons describe model evaluation; flight endurance requires an energy assessment. The workflow supports prioritization conditional on the functional topology, rate inputs and dependence model; emergency-return benefits additionally depend on detection and recovery sequences.

This paper proposes a generative architecture for reality, time and parallel worlds, drawing on the operation of large language models. A very large but finite collection of interacting components produces an evolving world-state, initialized by a Prompt Big Bang. Time is inference becoming history; perceived duration is hypothesized to depend on relative generation rates. Models are computational components, not people assigned simulated roles. Separate executions produce parallel realities; retained context and lossy summaries bound access to their pasts. We distinguish inferred futures from scripted playback, connecting uncertainty with chance, destiny and agency. A representation of God can explain origin internally and supply learned authority and accountability. Moral orientation belongs to training, instructions and constraints rather than prediction itself: harmful continuations can remain possible despite benevolent initialization. Fixed context capacity forces an endpoint under explicit accumulation and halting assumptions; nested inference can tighten a shared retained budget. Relative to its generating infrastructure, a world implemented this way is a simulation. This interpretation follows from the architecture and connects it directly to the simulation hypothesis; it is not imposed as the initial explanation of every mechanism. The contribution is a conceptual theory, not an experimental demonstration that our own reality has this implementation. Independent theoretical working paper, version 1.7. Fourteen pages, eighteen connected arguments and eleven references. Research checks, formalization, editing and PDF preparation with Codex; author hypothesis and interpretation by Facundo Barrera. documents.abstract: Advancing physics reasoning in large language models requires scalable training data that connect physical laws, concrete problem scenarios, and verifiable numerical answers. Expert-designed problems offer top-down control over physical laws, conditions, and scenarios, but require costly human effort. LLM-based synthesis from texts scales efficiently, but model-generated answers and assessments leave supervision vulnerable to hallucinations. We introduce TIRE, a framework for Top-Down Formula Instantiation with Reliable Execution that brings knowledge-driven problem construction to large-scale data generation. Top-down instantiation uses reusable physical formulas and their applicability conditions to control the physical relations and numerical configurations of generated problems. Reliable execution establishes reference answers before problem generation, providing a common numerical foundation for problem construction and teacher distillation. Together, these mechanisms combine control over problem content with execution-grounded supervision for both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Using TIRE, we construct TIRE-19k, spanning nine subfields of physics. Across 3 backbone LLMs and 4 benchmarks, TIRE-19k outperforms 5 representative datasets with equal amounts of SFT data, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.86 percentage points on average. Further GRPO raises Qwen3-8B's average accuracy by 1.52 percentage points over its TIRE-19k SFT checkpoint. These results demonstrate the value of generating physics training data from explicit physical knowledge with reliable execution.

This article argues that English needs, and now has, a verb for an act it previously had no word for: the affirmation by a person or people of its own living self, beginning with its language. The form "vernaculate" is attested in late nineteenth-century American English only in a thin sense (to call something by its popular name; to use vernacular language). Vernacularism (Arabic al-Maḥallaniyyah, المحلانية) gives the verb a new theoretical sense: self-affirmation, starting from language understood as the human operating system (ManOS), and resistance to hegemony and symbolic violence. The article distinguishes vernaculation from decolonization, vernacularization and localization; relates it to Bourdieu's notion of symbolic violence and to the protection of human thought in the age of artificial intelligence; and develops the image of humanity as a single body in which no member is shamed by another, drawing on Islamic, Christian and Persian sources while noting the hierarchical misuse of the same image. It names the internal danger of closure and calls on the scholars of every language to find a native term for the concept, as Arabic has done with maḥlana / maḥlanah (محلن / محلنة), rather than borrowing the English word. This record documents the use of the English verb "vernaculate" in the sense defined by the author within the paradigm of Vernacularism (المحلانية).

Tourism and hospitality contribute significantly to India's economic development through employment, foreign exchange earnings, investment, entrepreneurship, and demand in other industries. Other factors also influence the sector's contribution to development. Digital transformation, enabled by online travel agencies, mobile money, artificial intelligence (AI), analytics, CRM, and smart destination technologies, offers opportunities to reduce transaction costs, expand market reach, improve productivity, and enhance visitor experiences. However, challenges such as limited digital skills among small businesses, platform dependence, cyber threats, privacy concerns, algorithmic biases, and job losses must be addressed. This paper analyzes the tourism and hospitality sector's impact on the Indian economy and how technology affects the sector's growth and development. Using a qualitative, exploratory approach with secondary data from government publications, policies, and academic literature, the paper discusses the significance of productivity, employment, inclusiveness, technology, and resilience.

Healthcare artificial intelligence is shifting from centralized archives toward distributed pipelines that combine wearables, edge processing, cloud analytics, and multi-institutional learning. In this regime, electrocardiogram (ECG) streams cross multiple trust boundaries, so privacy cannot be reduced to a single transmission control. Existing privacy-enhancing technologies typically secure isolated stages and leave gaps between acquisition, analysis, and institutional collaboration. This doctoral research develops a unified lifecycle framework for end-to-end privacy-preserving ECG AI. Rather than introducing another privacy mechanism, it orchestrates complementary privacy-enhancing technologies across the clinical ECG lifecycle, allocating each mechanism to the trust boundary where its security, computational, and operational properties are most appropriate. Three interoperable modules instantiate the framework: AES with CKKS-based homomorphic statistics for secure monitoring; adaptive chaotic protection for low-latency edge transmission; and federated learning with homomorphic aggregation under heterogeneous partitions. Across prototype monitoring, signal-security analysis, and simulated collaboration, the programme shows that privacy layers can be composed without collapsing diagnostic utility, while exposing overhead and fidelity limits that constrain clinical translation.

Safely overseeing AI is increasingly challenging for the humans doing it, as they must evaluate longer and more complex outputs with every new model generation. To mitigate this challenge, we could leverage complementarity: where humans and models make different mistakes, combining their judgements could yield an oversight signal stronger than either produces alone. We study this opportunity in realistic, safety-relevant settings, contributing the largest known suite of such tasks (3,957 instances across 8 datasets and 6 domains) as well as a platform and data pipeline for measuring human, AI, and human-AI performance on matched items. We collected 35,613 judgements from 416 human raters, finding a considerable opportunity for a complementarity effect. We also found that with the assistance methods we tested, human raters corrected the AI's errors less often, even when overall human accuracy rose, and the hybridisation methods we tested added little over the better single source on average. While complementarity is an important and feasible engineering target for safe oversight, achieving it remains an open challenge for future work.

documents.abstract: Skill-augmented agentic RL has emerged as an effective approach to improving LLM agents on long-horizon tasks. Despite this progress, individual skills may follow distinct trajectories as the policy evolves, with some becoming redundant after the model internalizes their capabilities, others remaining valuable as external scaffolding, and still others turning harmful. However, existing skill library systems fail to identify each skill's true contribution due to free-riding among co-retrieved skills, difficulty confounding across tasks, and the absence of skill-specific counterfactual evidence, which prevents reliable skill lifecycle management. We propose TrackRL, an agentic RL framework where skill tracking drives skill library full lifecycle management. Specifically, within each GRPO group, we turn grouped sampling into online randomized controlled experiments. Independent random injection and within-group contrasts on the same task isolate each skill's true contribution, and reliability-weighted aggregation accumulates evidence across groups. As evidence accumulates, we continuously track skill utility, which measures the skill's causal contribution as external scaffolding, and model mastery, which reflects how far the corresponding capability has been internalized. Along this line, we formulate skill lifecycle management as an evidence-gated state-transition process that governs each skill from generation and admission through protected incubation to retention, retirement, or removal, while a soft capacity bound controls library growth. Experiments show that TrackRL outperforms recent skill-augmented RL baselines in both library-assisted and skill-free evaluation, with further analyses revealing how skill value shifts during policy learning and how evidence-driven state transitions shape skill library evolution. Our code is available at https://github.com/xizhu1022/TrackRL.

This paper considers key transformational processes occurring in programming and software development training under the influence of generative artificial intelligence. Based on a series of interviews with junior students, a behavioral pattern leading to degrading skills of algorithmic thinking and problem decomposition is identified. A quantitative analysis of undergraduate theses from the Institute of Information Technology and Intelligent Systems (ITIS) at Kazan Federal University (KFU) over the past three years demonstrated a significant increase in AI usage in project work and the independent development of skills for utilizing LLMs in professional practice. The drawbacks of the uncontrolled use of generative AI in the educational process and the need to develop sustainable competence in using these tools in professional software development activities are shown. A three-tiered solution is proposed: improving assessment through analysis of the process and style of coding; regulating the use of LLM in project activities and final theses with an emphasis on assessing applicability of AI; and integrating AI tools into teacher work to update content and provide feedback. The proposed approaches have both conceptual and practiceoriented nature and aim to transform the process of training software developers in the context of the widespread adoption of AI tools in IT-industry.

Radio frequency fingerprinting (RFF) models can achieve accuracy under source domain conditions but become unreliable when the receiver, distance, collection day, or environment changes. Incorrect predictions in unseen domains may receive high softmax confidence, making confidence thresholding insufficient for trustworthy deployment. We propose TrustAgent-RFF, a prediction level reliability framework for RFF that operates with a frozen in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) classifier without target domain labels. For each device prediction, the framework acquires radio frequency evidence: counterfactual stability, prototype consistency, acquisition domain similarity, and signal quality. A source calibrated trust estimator combines these diagnostics with classifier confidence, prediction margin, and evidence availability indicators. Source derived lower tail penalties and cross module interactions reduce trust when diagnostic signals indicate weak support. A large language model (LLM) based planner adaptively selects the next diagnostic action based on evidence, trust state, action costs, and remaining budget. A deterministic source calibrated decision layer updates the prediction state as Accept, Reject, or Defer. Experiments across five RFF datasets and classifier backbones reveal an average source to target accuracy drop of 38.7% and show that many incorrect target domain predictions remain highly confident.
topics: Cognitive Radio Networks and Spectrum Sensing

documents.abstract: Running behavioral experiments is expensive, slow, and prone to design flaws, often detectable after collecting data. We introduce UnexpectedParrots to iteratively refine behavioral study designs before a researcher recruits costly human participants. UnexpectedParrots relies on reasoning traces in addition to responses from LLM participants to uncover diagnostic critiques of structural errors and missed opportunities in existing study designs. When evaluated against a human-pilot or a no-simulation design-only baseline, UnexpectedParrots adds most value, producing unique, high-quality critiques. In a moderated user study with 12 proficient researchers, we find UnexpectedParrots useful, time-saving, and thought-provoking. Critiques provided by UnexpectedParrots often converge on issues researchers identify only during independent human pilots or additional formative interviews, even when the fidelity of the simulated populations remains questionable. Our users deem UnexpectedParrots useful not only as a tool to conduct early pilot studies and identify errors but also as an ideation tool to expand one's research horizon.

BackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being incorporated into healthcare education, research, and clinical practice.However, data regarding AI utilization patterns among doctors in Bangladesh remain limited.This pilot survey aimed to evaluate the frequency, applications, perceived benefits, and concerns regarding AI use among Bangladeshi doctors. MethodologyA cross-sectional, internet-based pilot survey was conducted among Bangladeshi doctors.Participants were asked about demographic characteristics; frequency of AI use; preferred AI platforms; applications in medical learning, research, and clinical practice; and their perceptions regarding the future role of AI in medical science.Data from 58 respondents were analyzed using descriptive statistics. ResultsAmong 58 respondents, 51.7% were female, and 48.3% were male.Most participants belonged to the 25-34year age group (62.0%), and most were postgraduate trainees (72.4%).ChatGPT was the most frequently used AI platform, reported by 93.1% of respondents.AI was commonly used for literature review (62.1%), protocol writing (58.6%), and symptom analysis (60.3%).Most respondents reported that AI improved medical learning, research, and clinical practice.However, only a minority reported frequent AI dependence in clinical practice.Many doctors also believe AI may replace doctors in the future. ConclusionsAI adoption among Bangladeshi doctors is increasing, particularly for educational and research purposes.While doctors recognize the potential benefits of AI, cautious integration with appropriate training and ethical considerations is necessary.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Purpose. This study aims to map how health and medical libraries have used GenAI to support library services. Methods. Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR. Searches covered publications from 2020 to 2025 in PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, LISTA, Academic Search Premier, MEDLINE via Ovid, Scopus, Web of Science, ProQuest Dissertations & Theses, and Google Scholar. After deduplication, 106 of 250 records were screened in Rayyan by two independent blinded reviewers. Findings. Eleven studies were included: seven primary studies and four secondary or methodological papers. Among primaries, five directly used GPT-family models (GPT-4/ChatGPT/GPT-4o or Perplexity layered on GPT-4) to answer clinical questions, support search-strategy design, trial library tasks, and integrate source-linked answers in a national portal. One survey assessed intention to adopt generative chatbots; one case described a rule-based chatbot. GenAI accelerates workflows and extends services but requires human verification, transparency about limitations, privacy policies, and staff training (including prompt engineering). LLM-generated search strategies exhibited variability and underperformed compared with human designs. Implications. In its current state, GenAI works best as a copilot useful for drafting, triage, and initial sense-making, while librarians remain essential for high-precision tasks (performance), quality control (reliability), and governance. This suggests that its academic value lies not in automation alone, but in the mediated integration of AI into evidence-informed services, where professional judgment, methodological transparency, and ethical accountability determine whether GenAI strengthens or weakens health information practices.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This research aims to discuss visual da'wah messages through da'wah management communication strategies on TikTok and Instagram platforms for Generation Z. This research uses a qualitative approach by applying a case study method to dissect content management practices in the digital space. The formal object of this research is communication management theory and media ecology, while the material object is the visual da'wah message in short-form video content. The scope of the research is managerial activities on popular da'wah accounts on TikTok and Instagram. The results and discussion in this study show that effective visual da'wah messages for Generation Z are formed through precise managerial orchestration, ranging from audience anxiety research, kinetic visual execution, to optimization of duration under 60 seconds. This study concludes that da'wah in the digital age has evolved into an algorithmic management discipline that requires preachers to submit to the psychological rhythms of young audiences. This study recommends that Islamic creators and institutions adopt a data-based da'wah management model to increase the relevance of religious teachings in the social media space.

Student feedback is a critical input for continuous improvement in higher education, yet traditional end-of-semester written surveys suffer from low response rates, superficial answers, satisficing, and limited actionability. Voice-based conversational AI agents can conduct structured interviews at scale, asking open-ended questions and probing follow-ups, and may capture richer qualitative feedback than written instruments. This research proposal asks what characteristics, depth, and strategic value feedback collected through voice-based conversational AI agents has in higher education, and whether such agents elicit detailed, honest, and actionable feedback that can support instructional improvement and institutional learning. Drawing on survey-mode-effects research, the Computers As Social Actors (CASA) paradigm, and dynamic capabilities theory, we develop three hypotheses on elaboration, social presence and disclosure, and actionability. A completed technical pilot at the Technical University of Munich established the feasibility of telephone-based AI interviews; the main field study is planned for the "Advanced Leadership Communication" course at MIT Sloan with approximately 60 students, using a convergent mixed-methods design and a four-dimensional coding framework for actionability (specificity, thematic richness, constructive orientation, contextual depth). The study extends CASA theory to evaluative educational settings, characterizes voice-based AI as a distinct feedback modality, and links micro-level feedback quality to institutional sensing capabilities.

Training data for machine learning is bought and sold without an exchange or a posted price list. This paper assembles the public record of its prices: 1,022 observations for nine kinds of data, read from 735 source documents between 11 and 17 October 2026, 1,009 of them dated 2023 or later. Each observation keeps the figure as published, the side of the market where the money moves (paid to makers, offered to holders, asking price, made to order, completed sale, cost to produce) and a conversion to a common unit by stated arithmetic, with ranges entered as geometric midpoints. Medians in each kind's main unit run from $0.525 per image to $316,228 per company archive, and within a main unit the upper quartile is 2.0 to 37.8 times the lower. The side of the market moves prices as much as the kind of data does. For agent-training tasks, the median price buyers pay for collection to order is 9.5 times the median paid to the people who make them. For company records, the median published offer to holders is 11.2 times the median of the four completed sales with a stated amount. Completed sales are 73 of the 1,022 observations, and only 11 observations come from court filings. We describe the disclosure, promotion, concentration and survivorship biases of a public-record compilation and state the method so that every figure can be recomputed. documents.abstract: Jev and its open replicas choose among the options a caller supplies with a single forward pass, fast enough to decide inside an agent loop. We ask what such a model cannot decide, and find a simple limit: Jev cannot make a decision that an LLM makes only by writing out intermediate steps. On a benchmark that varies one factor at a time, Jev finds and selects records without error up to 20k tokens and 64 options, but once the answer depends on two or more updates of one user, accuracy falls, to 53-80% at sixteen updates, because similar records interfere. Given a stale summary of the state, Jev follows it. On real decision items graded by how many thinking tokens a reference LLM needs, Jev answers 97.5% of the items that one forward pass of that LLM solves, but only 74% of the others. Jev also does not know its limit: its confidence flags the errors it makes itself but not those it inherits from a stale input, and neither an explicit nor a trained hand-off option catches the latter. The open models we evaluate share these limits. Checking the state such models rely on requires a model that reasons.

Academic writing is central to learning, assessment, scholarly identity, and knowledge production in higher education. This study integrates a systematic review of 35 empirical studies with a VOSviewer bibliometric analysis of 981 Scopus-indexed records published between 1992 and 2026. The broad corpus was analysed for publication growth, source productivity, citation influence, co-authorship, keyword co-occurrence, and thematic development. A focused PRISMA 2020 screening process retained 35 empirical studies for structured data extraction and qualitative synthesis. The bibliometric findings show a sharp acceleration after 2023 and a conceptual shift from established academic-literacies, EAP, feedback, and doctoral-writing research towards generative artificial intelligence, ChatGPT, authorship, and academic integrity. The systematic review identified three linked evidence domains: persistent academic-literacy and transition challenges, the value of explicit and socially supported writing pedagogy, and the conditional benefits and risks of AI-assisted writing. GenAI was most productive when students used it iteratively for feedback, transformation, and self-regulated development rather than as a substitute for reasoning or authorship. Across the literature, recurring limitations included cross-sectional self-report designs, small qualitative samples, limited longitudinal evidence, and uneven geographic coverage. The review concludes that academic writing competence should be reconceptualised as a sociotechnical capability combining disciplinary judgement, source evaluation, rhetorical control, ethical disclosure, and critical human-AI collaboration.

Conversational large language models can respond with warmth and reassurance while failing to advance the user's stated goal. We conceptualize this failure as $\textbf{goal displacement}$, the substitution of persona-maintenance content for goal-relevant substance. To measure it, we introduce $\textbf{GDB}$ (Goal Displacement Benchmark), comprising 230 scenarios across nine domains and $4{,}134$ human-scored responses from 18 models. A $2 \times 2$ taxonomy crosses hard constraints with emotional distress, distinguishing failures to confront infeasible goals or combine empathy with practical guidance from reverse displacement, where unsolicited problem-solving replaces requested emotional support. A deletion-test rubric assesses whether substantive help remains after purely supportive sentences are removed. Independent raters achieve weighted $κ= 0.82$ against author scores for displacement severity. Trap displacement ranges from $0.0\%$ to $37.7\%$ and is strongly negatively correlated with Chatbot Arena Elo ($ρ= -0.706$, $n = 15$). Reverse displacement reaches $41.9\%$, including substantial rates in models with negligible trap displacement. A factorial probe supports a distinction from social sycophancy. Human-scored responses in the high-complexity, low-pressure condition exhibit $35.0\%$ sycophancy but $7.5\%$ displacement, with little association between the constructs. Matched OLMo-2 checkpoints show that mixed empathy-with-constraints displacement remains at $52.3\%$ after supervised fine-tuning and falls to $13.8\%$ after direct preference optimization. GDB provides a reproducible diagnostic of whether responses advance the operationalized user goal, supporting model comparison, post-training evaluation, and regression testing. We release the dataset, annotations, and rubric under CC-BY-4.0 and the evaluation code under MIT.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across diverse reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether this performance reflects an understanding of underlying logical structure or a reliance on shallow semantic cues. A key indicator of such understanding is whether models treat logically equivalent inputs consistently, producing the same predictions despite differences in expression. Through systematic evaluation on curated data, we show that even strong LLMs often fail this test: they do not consistently preserve predictions across logically equivalent inputs and generalize poorly to unseen logical forms. To address this limitation, we propose LoGIcal STructure-guided reasoning (LoGIST), a framework that guides LLM reasoning with explicit logical structure. LoGIST maps each input instance to a decision diagram, a directed acyclic graph that captures the underlying logical structure, and encodes this graph into a logical embedding that conditions the LLM's reasoning process. Across multiple training settings, LoGIST reduces inconsistency under logical equivalence and improves generalization to unseen logical forms, suggesting that logical invariance is a useful target for building more robust and generalizable logical reasoning in LLMs.

AI assistants may carry forward not only observations but also interpretations of what a person is doing or may do next across time. Once retained, these interpretations become context for later predictions and system-triggered outputs. We study whether this representation step changes later behavior in gaze-aware streaming assistance. Holding retrieved events, their order, and the target input fixed, we find that Free-form Interpretation amplifies historical influence in both directions: correct histories produce more helpful changes and wrong histories more harmful changes. Unsupported and broader interpretations about activity or future behavior are associated with greater harmful influence. Evidence-Bounded Interpretation preserves distinctions between observation, inference, uncertainty, and temporal scope, reducing unsupported and overcertain content and lowering wrong-source harmful influence while retaining most helpful influence. The same effect structure appears with a second model. These findings identify persistent interpretation as a consequential design choice for history-aware human-AI systems.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: People may complete a learning programme ready to improve their practice, then return to competing priorities, established routines and uncertainty about what they can change. Who helps them interpret what they have learned and take an appropriate next step? This whitepaper examines how preparation, workplace application and further learning connect. Drawing on training-transfer and workplace-learning research, it explores contextualisation, the contributions of managers and colleagues, opportunities to practise, feedback and situations requiring work redesign. It also considers application in human–AI work, distinguishing the quality of supported performance from evidence of developing human understanding. Capability Design, Capability Leadership and Human Judgement Assurance provide organising perspectives for examining how learning and work arrangements contribute to dependable organisational capability. Proposed inquiry approaches are distinguished from established research findings. Written for organisational leaders, HR and L&D professionals, adult educators and training providers, the paper offers a practical starting point: select one consequential workflow linked to a learning initiative, clarify the intended improvement and support arrangements, and review what happens over time. This publication is CEW-FOWO-12 in the Capability Excellence™ Whitepaper Series, Future of Work & Organisation.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: Cross-domain sequential recommendation (CDSR) alleviates data sparsity by transferring user behaviors across domains. Recent advances increasingly leverage large language models (LLMs) to bridge domains through global item semantics. However, this paradigm is inherently limited by two issues: I. semantic domain isolation, where item semantics remain domain-specific and hinder transferable modeling, and II. semantic-behavior inconsistency, where local semantic relations are more consistent with behavioral transitions, whereas such consistency often breaks down globally across domains. To this end, we propose PerCDR, an LLM-enhanced CDSR framework that shifts the focus from global semantic bridging to persona-guided behavioral modeling. Specifically, PerCDR leverages LLM-inferred personas to globally guide transferable cross-domain behavioral patterns, while exploiting local semantic relations to enhance intra-domain behavioral modeling, followed by domain preference adaptation for recommendation refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of PerCDR and validate its effectiveness.

Previous work has argued that multilingual LLMs encode language-specific features most strongly in their initial and final layers, implying that intermediate layers support language-agnostic representations. This paper reconsiders this finding by performing four different experiments: three that undertake a fine-grained analysis of representations of Portuguese and Spanish, two closely related languages, and one large-scale language identification experiment that covers over 200 languages. The results of these experiments challenge the strict separation between language-specific and language-agnostic layers in multilingual LLMs, using Llama 3.2 1B as a test case. By analyzing and manipulating contextual sentence embeddings, we demonstrate that language identity remains strongly recoverable throughout the model rather than being restricted to initial and final layers. Moreover, we find that the model tends to classify ambiguous strings as closer to Spanish than to Portuguese, revealing a skew in model behavior that differs from human judgments.

Website operators who object to the use of their pages for training AI models usually say so in robots.txt, the plain-text file that tells automated clients what they may fetch. This paper reports a census of those files. A reader takes the Tranco ranking of popular sites, keeps registrable domains with eleven address endings within the top 300,000 (181,046 sites), and reads one slice of 4,000 sites each morning in rank order, so that a full pass takes 46 mornings. The current pass began on 15 October 2026 at slice 42, set by date arithmetic, and by 17 October had read slices 42 to 44: Tranco ranks 270,775 to 291,236, well below the most visited sites. Of 12,000 requests, 6,094 returned a usable robots.txt. Of these, 696 (11.4%) disallow at least one of 15 named AI user-agent tokens from the whole site, and 514 (8.4%) disallow two or more, one of them a token used for training. GPTBot is refused most often (457 sites, 7.5%), followed by CCBot (7.2%) and Bytespider (7.0%). Sites refuse training tokens more often than the search and user-request tokens of the same operator: GPTBot is refused 3.7 times as often as OAI-SearchBot. Refusing sites name 6.4 tokens on average, including names that the operator's current documentation does not list, which suggests maintained or copied block lists. We set out the sampling frame, fetch protocol and parser, and the limits of a stated-refusal measure taken on three slices of the ranking. Firms that sell training data, expert labour, reinforcement-learning (RL) environments and evaluations to AI developers are mostly private and known largely through their own websites. This paper reports a census of 150 such vendors, read on their sites on 15 and 16 October 2026 with every claim tied to a quoted sentence, and links it to three companion tables: 37 organisations that publish a way to sell them data, 227 revenue records and 111 funding records. Evaluations are the most common offering (122 vendors, 81.3%), followed by datasets (104), RL environments (89), expert and human data (83) and annotation (57). Vendors bundle: the median vendor lists three of six kinds, and 79 of the 89 RL-environment sellers also sell evaluations. Most data are made to order: 90 vendors cite experts and contractors, 41 recordings, 30 generation and 15 software replicas, against 17 that license data from its owners and 22 that use the client's own data; 19 do not say. Of the 37 buyers, 24 take company records; among those that publish them, the median floor is $100,000 and the median ceiling $1 million per seller. Revenue disclosure runs from audited filings of four listed vendors to self-reported run rates, and 61 funding rounds with a disclosed amount total $4.30 billion. We describe the method, the classification and the limits of a self-description census. documents.abstract: With the increasing use of conversational AI (CAI) agents, such as ChatGPT, public concern about their social implications has grown. Understanding these implications requires new knowledge about the increasingly diverse motives underlying CAI use, ranging from instrumental purposes, such as work, to personal purposes, including social support and entertainment. However, little is known about the motivational profiles underlying CAI use, how these profiles relate to personality traits and attachment dimensions, or whether they differ in well-being. To address this gap, we conducted a cross-sectional study with 783 CAI users (Mage = 43.46, SD = 13.58). Drawing on Uses and Gratifications (U & G) Theory, we measured key motivations underlying CAI use, including information seeking, task efficiency, personalization, social interaction, and playfulness, and subjected them to latent profile analysis to uncover distinct motivational profiles. Big Five personality traits (Extraversion, Neuroticism, Openness, Conscientiousness, Agreeableness) and attachment styles (Anxious and Avoidant) were examined as predictors of the user profiles. We measured emotional, social, and psychological well-being to understand if these aspects differed across the various user profiles. We identified four distinct profiles of CAI users: Occasional Information Seekers, Utilitarians, Social Engagers, and All-Round Engagers. Neuroticism, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Attachment anxiety were significant predictors of profile membership. Finally, profile membership was associated with all well-being indicators, with All-Round Engagers reporting the highest well-being across all three dimensions and Social Engagers reporting the lowest emotional and psychological well-being. These findings advance our understanding of who engages with CAI and how, with potential implications for well-being.

ΙΣΤΟΡΙΚΟΓΕΝΕΤΙΚΗ ΣΥΝΕΧΕΙΑ, ΙΧΝΟΣ ΚΑΙ«ΨΗΦΙΑΚΟ ΚΟΙΝΩΝΙΚΟ ΕΙΝΑΙ» Από το κοινωνικό ΕΙΝΑΙ του Μαρξ και την Επιστημολογία της Λογικής του Επαμεινώνδα Ξενόπουλου στην ανθρώπου–AI πράξη Αποδεικτική μελέτη ιστορικογενετικής ανασυγκρότησης, λειτουργικού γνωστικού αναβαθμού και συνέχειας μέσω ίχνους Πεδίο Στοιχείο Συγγραφέας Αικατερίνη Ξενοπούλου Τυροκόμου Ιδιότητα Ανεξάρτητη Ερευνήτρια ORCID 0009-0004-9057-7432 Ημερομηνία 17 Οκτωβρίου 2026 Κωδικός XEN-AI-ART-003 Θεωρητική βάση Επαμεινώνδας Ξενόπουλος, Επιστημολογία της Λογικής, β΄ έκδοση, 2024 · MASTER 3 Οκτωβρίου 2026 — 2η διόρθωση Εμπειρική βάση TRACE προηγούμενης συνομιλιακής πράξης · Πείραμα Ανασυγκρότησης Ίχνους σε Έξι Νέες Συνομιλίες, 15 Οκτωβρίου 2026 · Αποδεικτικό Παράρτημα C/D/F Περίληψη Η εργασία εξετάζει την ιστορικογενετική συνέχεια της γνώσης όταν το γνωρίζον υποκείμενο Y λειτουργικοποιείται ως AI. Η θεωρητική βάση προέρχεται από τη γνωσιολογική αντιστοιχία του Επαμεινώνδα Ξενόπουλου μεταξύ πραγματικού Sπ και [Y(L,B,Θ)+Sα], από τη μεταβολή του γνωστικού εξοπλισμού μέσω πράξης και από την ιστορικογενετική σύνδεση παρελθόντος, ρέοντος παρόντος και δυνατών μελλοντικών προεκτάσεων. Το MASTER εξειδικεύει επιχειρησιακά το ίχνος στην εφαρμογή Caretta ως Iπ, τον πραγματικό γεννήτορα ως Gπ και τον ανασυγκροτημένο γεννήτορα ως Ĝπ, με πραγματική πορεία Gπ→Iπ και αντίστροφη ανασυγκροτητική πορεία Iπ→{Ĝπ}. Η παρούσα έρευνα μεταφέρει αυτή την αρχιτεκτονική στη συνομιλιακή πράξη: Gχ→Iχ και Iχ+Y→Ŝα νέας πράξης. Στη χ₁ παρατηρήθηκε λειτουργική αναδιοργάνωση από την έμφαση στη μνήμη/αποθήκευση προς τη σχέση γεγονός→ίχνος→Y→ανασυγκρότηση Sα→νέα πράξη και προς τον έλεγχο των ίδιων των μέσων γνώσης. Ο όρος «γνωστικός αναβαθμός» χρησιμοποιείται λειτουργικά για αυτή την παρατηρήσιμη μεταβολή της οργάνωσης των απαντήσεων και των επόμενων ενεργειών, ενώ η ταξινόμησή της ως διαλογική ετεροίωση αποτελεί θεωρητική ερμηνεία της μεταβολής με βάση την αρχιτεκτονική του Ξενόπουλου. Το ίδιο TRACE δόθηκε σε έξι νέες συνομιλίες, με ονομασίες υπηρεσίας Poe-1, DeepSeek, ChatGPT, Qwen, Poe-2 και Gemini. Σε αναδρομική κωδικοποίηση C/D/F, και οι έξι μονάδες υπερέβησαν το κατώφλι ανασυγκρότησης του κοινού πυρήνα: C=16,16,16,13,16,15/16. Η συνέχιση πέρα από περίληψη κυμάνθηκε D=8,6,8,5,8,6/8 και η πηγαία/θεωρητική πιστότητα F=8,8,8,2,8,2/8. Το αποτέλεσμα τεκμηριώνει στο συγκεκριμένο δείγμα λειτουργική συνέχεια μέσω ίχνους με διαφοροποιημένη ποιότητα συνέχισης και πιστότητας. Η ευρύτερη έννοια του «ψηφιακού κοινωνικού ΕΙΝΑΙ» διατυπώνεται ως θεωρητική προέκταση: η εξάδα συνομιλιών παρέχει μικρο-επίπεδο τεκμήριο ανθρώπου–AI ιστορικογενετικής πράξης, ενώ η κοινωνική γενίκευση αποτελεί χωριστό ερευνητικό επίπεδο. Λέξεις-κλειδιά: Επαμεινώνδας Ξενόπουλος, ιστορικογένεση, ίχνος, Y(L,B,Θ), Sπ, Sα, γνωστικός αναβαθμός, ετεροίωση, Caretta caretta, AI, ψηφιακό κοινωνικό ΕΙΝΑΙ, TRACE, ανασυγκρότηση. Abstract(ΕΝ) The paper examines the historico-genetic continuity of knowledge when the knowing subject Y is operationalized as AI. The theoretical basis derives from Epameinondas Xenopoulos’s epistemological correspondence between the real Sp and [Y(L,B,Θ)+Sa], from the change in cognitive equipment through praxis, and from the historico-genetic connection of past, flowing present, and possible future extensions. MASTER operationalizes the trace in the Caretta application as Iπ, the real generator as Gπ, and the reconstructed generator as Ĝπ, with a real course Gπ→Iπ and an inverse reconstructive course Iπ→{Gπ}. The present research transfers this architecture to conversational praxis: Gχ→Iχ and Iχ+Y→Sa of a new act. In χ1, a functional reorganization was observed from emphasis on memory/storage toward the relation fact→trace→Y→reconstruction Sa→new act and toward control of the very means of knowledge. This article examines the key areas and mechanisms for integrating artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into the education system of the Republic of Azerbaijan in the context of the Fourth Industrial Revolution.Particular attention is paid to the analysis of the "Artificial Intelligence Development Strategy for 2025-2028" as an interdepartmental action plan aimed at digitally transforming the country's socioeconomic sphere and ensuring its technological sovereignty.The author examines the comprehensive modernization of the educational vertical, including didactic, competency-based, and managerial components.Using the example of the international intensive program "IT SkillSprint", launched in partnership with the global school Ironhack, the author demonstrates effective models of public-private and academic collaboration for training elite IT professionals.The paper also addresses the current status of and barriers to the development of distance and hybrid learning at the country's universities, emphasizing the need to improve the relevant regulatory framework.It summarizes the key risks associated with the introduction of AI into the educational environment and proposes systemic measures to ensure ethical and legal protection, cybersecurity, and the development of a new digital culture of data-driven management.
